text: Once you've found the claim that matters, the next step is trying to produce it yourself. This is slower and more humbling than it sounds — most researchers who attempt a serious reproduction uncover gaps between the paper and reality that the paper itself never mentions.

Start from the authors' own released code and checkpoints, not a blank reimplementation — the code is the ground truth of what was actually run, while the paper is a lossy summary of it. Run their exact scripts before changing anything. Only once the official code works should you move to your own reimplementation, because debugging a reimplementation against the paper's number directly leaves you unable to tell a bug in your code from a real discrepancy in the result.

Match hyperparameters exactly, not approximately — optimizer settings, learning rate schedule, warmup, and data preprocessing — and pin your random seed, disabling nondeterministic GPU kernels along the way. It won't guarantee identical numbers across different hardware, but it removes one entire axis of variation from your own attempt.

There's no single standard for "reproduced." An exact match within noise is the strongest claim and needs known variance to even evaluate fairly. A match within tolerance means the practical conclusion doesn't change even if the exact digits differ. A qualitative trend match, often run at a smaller compute budget than the original, is weaker but still informative — as long as you're honest with yourself about which one you actually attempted.
Many of the gaps that cause a reproduction to fail aren't mysterious at all — they're a known, recurring set of pitfalls, which the next lesson walks through directly, one at a time.
